title: Sigma and pi bonds, and hybridization
summary: A covalent bond forms where two orbitals overlap. Head-on overlap gives a [[sigma-bond|sigma bond]]; sideways overlap of p orbitals gives a [[pi-bond|pi bond]], usually weaker. [[hybridization|Hybridization]] links the [[electron-domain|electron domains]] around an atom to the orbitals it bonds with, so each one predicts the other.

goals.text: Describe how sigma bonds and pi bonds form, and where their electron density lies.
Deduce the number of sigma and pi bonds in a molecule or ion from its Lewis formula.
Explain sp³, sp² and sp hybridization, including which orbitals mix and which are left over.
Link Lewis formula, electron domains, geometry and hybridization, and predict each one from the others.

before.prompt: How many unpaired electrons does a carbon atom have in its ground state?
before.hint: Fill the 2p orbitals one electron each first.
before.explain: Carbon is $\mathrm{1s^{2}\,2s^{2}\,2p^{2}}$. The two 2p electrons sit in separate orbitals, so two are unpaired. Revise it in {{lesson:1.4}}.

before.prompt: Carbonyl sulfide has the Lewis formula $\ce{O=C=S}$, with no lone pairs on carbon. How many electron domains are there around the carbon atom?
before.hint: A double bond counts as one domain.
before.explain: Each double bond is one domain and carbon has no lone pair, so there are two. Revise it in {{lesson:2.3}}.

before.prompt: Which of these is a [[polar-molecule|polar molecule]]?
before.hint: Polar bonds are not enough: the shape must stop the dipoles cancelling.
before.explain: All four have polar bonds, but only in the bent shape do the dipoles not cancel. Revise it in {{lesson:2.4}}.

blocks.text: A [[covalent-bond|covalent bond]] is a shared pair of electrons. Usually each atom offers an [[atomic-orbital|atomic orbital]] holding one electron (in a coordination bond, one orbital brings both), the two orbitals overlap, and the pair sits in the overlap.
The line through the two nuclei is the bond axis. Orbitals can overlap head-on, along that axis, or sideways, beside it.

blocks.statement: A covalent bond formed by head-on overlap of two orbitals, with most of its electron density on the bond axis, between the nuclei.
blocks.plain: The orbitals point straight at each other, and the pair sits between the atoms.

blocks.statement: A covalent bond formed by sideways overlap of two parallel p orbitals, with its electron density on opposite sides of the bond axis.
blocks.plain: Two side-by-side p orbitals merge above and below the line joining the atoms.

blocks.alt: Three rows, each with a dashed horizontal bond axis through two nuclei. Top row: two spherical s orbitals overlap on the axis between the nuclei, labelled sigma bond, s and s overlap, head-on along the axis. Middle row: two dumbbell-shaped p orbitals lie along the axis and their inner lobes overlap between the nuclei, labelled sigma bond, p and p overlap, head-on along the axis. Bottom row: two p orbitals stand upright, parallel to each other and at right angles to the axis; they overlap in one region above the axis and one below it, labelled pi bond, parallel p orbitals, sideways, above and below the axis.
blocks.caption: Head-on overlap puts the shared pair on the axis ($\sigma$). Sideways overlap puts it above and below the axis ($\pi$).

blocks.text: Any two orbitals can overlap head-on: s with s in $\ce{H2}$, s with p in $\ce{HCl}$, p with p in $\ce{Cl2}$. So the first bond between two atoms is always a [[sigma-bond|sigma bond]] ($\sigma$).
A [[pi-bond|pi bond]], written $\pi$, needs two parallel p orbitals at right angles to the axis. They only get close enough once a $\sigma$ bond holds the atoms together.

blocks.statement: A single bond is one $\sigma$ bond. A double bond is one $\sigma$ bond and one $\pi$ bond. A triple bond is one $\sigma$ bond and two $\pi$ bonds.
blocks.why: Only one head-on overlap fits on the axis, so extra bonds overlap sideways, at right angles to each other.

blocks.text: Sideways overlap is less effective, so a $\pi$ bond is usually weaker than a $\sigma$ bond. Its exposed electrons are why alkenes react at the double bond.

blocks.question: Use the carbon–carbon bond enthalpies in section 12 of the data booklet to estimate the energy needed to break the $\pi$ bond in $\ce{C=C}$.
steps: $\ce{C-C}$ is one $\sigma$ bond: $\pu{346 kJ mol-1}$. $\ce{C=C}$ is one $\sigma$ plus one $\pi$: $\pu{614 kJ mol-1}$.
Take away the $\sigma$ bond: $614 - 346 = \pu{268 kJ mol-1}$.
Sense check: $268 < 346$, so the $\pi$ bond is the weaker one. It is an estimate, because bond enthalpies are averages.

blocks.question: Propenal, $\ce{CH2=CHCHO}$, is an aldehyde with a $\ce{C=C}$ double bond. Deduce the number of $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds in one molecule.
steps: Draw every bond: $\ce{H2C=CH-CH=O}$, with one hydrogen on each of carbons 2 and 3.
Single bonds, one $\sigma$ each: four $\ce{C-H}$ and one $\ce{C-C}$, so 5 $\sigma$.
Double bonds, $\sigma + \pi$ each: $\ce{C=C}$ and $\ce{C=O}$, so 2 $\sigma$ and 2 $\pi$.
Check: 8 atoms with no ring need $8 - 1 = 7$ $\sigma$ bonds to join them.
blocks.answer: Propenal has 7 σ bonds and 2 π bonds.

blocks.text: Missing the $\ce{C-H}$ bonds when counting from a condensed or skeletal formula. Draw every bond first: each $\ce{C-H}$ is one $\sigma$ bond.

blocks.prompt: How many $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds are there in one molecule of hydrogen cyanide, $\ce{HCN}$?
blocks.hint: Draw $\ce{H-C#N}$. A triple bond holds only one $\sigma$ bond.
blocks.explain: $\ce{H-C}$ is one $\sigma$; $\ce{C#N}$ is one $\sigma$ and two $\pi$.

blocks.prompt: Where is the electron density of a $\pi$ bond concentrated?
blocks.hint: Picture two upright p orbitals side by side.

options.text: above and below the bond axis
on the bond axis, between the nuclei

blocks.explain: The parallel p orbitals overlap above and below the axis. Density on the axis is a $\sigma$ bond.

verify.truth: above and below the bond axis

blocks.text: Carbon, $\mathrm{1s^{2}\,2s^{2}\,2p^{2}}$, has only two unpaired electrons. Yet methane has four identical $\ce{C-H}$ bonds, $109.5^{\circ}$ apart, and the 2p orbitals are only $90^{\circ}$ apart.
The model fixes this in two steps. One 2s electron is promoted into the empty 2p orbital. Then the 2s and three 2p orbitals mix into four identical orbitals.

blocks.statement: The mixing of atomic orbitals on one atom to give a set of new, equivalent hybrid orbitals that the atom uses for bonding.
blocks.plain: An atom blends its s and p orbitals into identical orbitals that point where its bonds go.

blocks.text: In [[hybridization|hybridization]], the number of hybrid orbitals equals the number of orbitals mixed: sp³ is one s and three p.

blocks.alt: Orbital boxes for carbon's valence electrons, five rows. Ground state: 2s box with an up and a down arrow, then three 2p boxes with one up arrow in each of the first two and the third empty. Below that, 2s electron promoted: 2s box with one up arrow, and three 2p boxes each with one up arrow. A dashed line separates the hybrid rows. sp3, four domains: four hybrid boxes, each with one up arrow. sp2, three domains: three hybrid boxes with one up arrow each, then one separate p box with one up arrow. sp, two domains: two hybrid boxes with one up arrow each, then two separate p boxes with one up arrow each.
blocks.caption: Promotion gives carbon four unpaired electrons. Mixing four, three or two of its orbitals gives the sp³, sp² or sp set; any p orbitals left over can form $\pi$ bonds.

blocks.text: [[sp3-hybridization|sp³ hybridization]]: one s and three p orbitals give four sp³ orbitals, pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron, $109.5^{\circ}$ apart. Each forms a $\sigma$ bond or holds a lone pair.

[[sp2-hybridization|sp² hybridization]]: one s and two p orbitals give three sp² orbitals in a plane, $120^{\circ}$ apart. The leftover p orbital, at right angles to the plane, can form one $\pi$ bond.
sp hybridization: one s and one p orbital give two sp orbitals in a line, $180^{\circ}$ apart. The two leftover p orbitals can form two $\pi$ bonds.
Lone pairs sit in hybrid orbitals too: ammonia's nitrogen is sp³, with three $\sigma$ bonds and a lone pair. Only sp, sp² and sp³ are needed in this course.

blocks.question: Explain how hybridization accounts for the four identical $\ce{C-H}$ bonds in methane, $\ce{CH4}$.
steps: Promotion: carbon gets four unpaired electrons.
Mixing: 2s and three 2p give four equivalent sp³ orbitals.
Shape: tetrahedral, $109.5^{\circ}$.
Bonds: each sp³ orbital overlaps head-on with a hydrogen 1s orbital.
blocks.answer: One 2s electron of carbon is promoted to the empty 2p orbital, giving four unpaired electrons. The 2s orbital and the three 2p orbitals mix to form four equivalent sp³ hybrid orbitals. These point to the corners of a tetrahedron, $109.5^{\circ}$ apart. Each sp³ orbital overlaps head-on with a hydrogen 1s orbital, so methane has four identical σ bonds.

verify.truth: promotion, mixing into four equivalent sp3 orbitals, tetrahedral 109.5, four sigma bonds

blocks.alt: Ethene drawn on a flat tilted plane. Two carbon atoms joined by a single line labelled sigma lie in the plane; each carbon also bonds to two hydrogen atoms in the same plane. One sausage-shaped cloud sits above the plane over both carbons, labelled pi bond above the plane, and a matching cloud sits below it, labelled pi bond below the plane. A note reads: each carbon is sp2, three sigma bonds at 120 degrees, one p orbital in the pi bond.
blocks.caption: In ethene the $\sigma$ framework is flat. The $\pi$ bond is one bond with two halves, above and below the plane.

blocks.question: Describe the bonding between the two carbon atoms in ethene, $\ce{C2H4}$, in terms of hybridization and $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds.
steps: Each carbon has three domains and no lone pair, so it is sp².
$\sigma$ bond: head-on overlap of an sp² orbital from each carbon.
$\pi$ bond: sideways overlap of the two parallel unhybridized p orbitals.
blocks.answer: Each carbon atom is sp² hybridized, with three sp² orbitals in a plane at $120^{\circ}$ and one unhybridized p orbital. One sp² orbital on each carbon overlaps head-on to form the σ bond between the carbons. The two unhybridized p orbitals are parallel and overlap sideways to form a π bond. The π electron density lies above and below the plane of the molecule.

verify.truth: sp2 carbons; sp2-sp2 head-on sigma; sideways p-p pi above and below the plane
forbids: two σ bonds between the carbons

blocks.prompt: How many unhybridized p orbitals does an sp hybridized carbon atom have?
blocks.hint: Carbon has three 2p orbitals. How many of them went into the sp set?
blocks.explain: sp uses one s and one p orbital, leaving two 2p orbitals for two $\pi$ bonds.

blocks.prompt: What is the hybridization of the nitrogen atom in ammonia, $\ce{NH3}$?
blocks.hint: Count the lone pair as well as the three bonds.
blocks.explain: Three bonds and one lone pair make four domains, so sp³. sp² comes from forgetting the lone pair.

sections.heading: From Lewis formula to hybridization, and back

blocks.text: Hybridization follows from the [[electron-domain|electron domains]] you count for the [[vsepr-model|VSEPR model]] in {{lesson:2.3}}.
1. Draw the Lewis formula, with every lone pair.
2. Count the electron domains on the atom: each lone pair and each bond is one domain, whether single, double or triple.
3. Read off the hybridization: four domains, sp³; three domains, sp²; two domains, sp.

4. The [[electron-domain-geometry|electron domain geometry]] matches the hybrid set: tetrahedral for sp³, trigonal planar for sp², linear for sp. Lone pairs then set the [[molecular-geometry|molecular geometry]], as in VSEPR.

blocks.statement: For an atom with two, three or four electron domains: number of hybrid orbitals = number of electron domains = $\sigma$ bonds + lone pairs on that atom. $\pi$ bonds are not counted.
blocks.why: Each $\sigma$ bond and each lone pair needs its own hybrid orbital, but a $\pi$ bond is made from a leftover p orbital.

blocks.text: It works backwards too. An sp² atom has trigonal planar domains, about $120^{\circ}$ apart, and one p orbital free for a $\pi$ bond.

blocks.question: Pent-1-en-4-yne is $\ce{CH2=CH-CH2-C#CH}$. Number its carbon atoms 1 to 5 from the left, and deduce the hybridization of each one.
steps: Carbon 1: two $\ce{C-H}$ and the double bond, three domains.
Carbon 2: one $\ce{C-H}$, the double bond and a single bond, three domains.
Carbon 3: four single bonds, four domains.
Carbons 4 and 5: the triple bond and one single bond each, two domains.
blocks.answer: Carbons 1 and 2 are sp², carbon 3 is sp³, and carbons 4 and 5 are sp.

verify.truth: C1 sp2, C2 sp2, C3 sp3, C4 sp, C5 sp

blocks.question: For the carbonate ion, $\ce{CO3^2-}$, deduce the number of $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds in one Lewis formula, the hybridization of carbon and the shape of the ion.
steps: $4 + 3(6) + 2 = 24$ valence electrons: one $\ce{C=O}$ and two $\ce{C-O^-}$ in one Lewis formula.
Each carbon–oxygen bond has one $\sigma$; the double bond adds one $\pi$.
Carbon has three domains and no lone pair. Resonance spreads the $\pi$ electrons ({{lesson:2.8}}), but carbon stays sp².
blocks.answer: One Lewis formula has 3 σ bonds and 1 π bond. Carbon has three electron domains and no lone pairs, so it is sp² hybridized. The ion is trigonal planar, with bond angles of $120^{\circ}$.

blocks.text: Hybridization gives the shape, and the shape settles polarity. Boron in $\ce{BF3}$ has three domains and no lone pair: sp², trigonal planar. Its leftover p orbital is empty, so there is no $\pi$ bond.
The three polar $\ce{B-F}$ bonds cancel, so $\ce{BF3}$ is not a [[polar-molecule|polar molecule]].
When you "deduce" a hybridization, write the domain count first: "four electron domains, so sp³". It shows your reasoning and catches lone pairs.

blocks.prompt: An atom is sp hybridized and has no lone pairs. What are its molecular geometry and bond angle?
blocks.hint: How many hybrid orbitals does sp give, and how far apart are they?
blocks.explain: sp gives two hybrid orbitals, so two domains. With no lone pairs they point opposite ways: linear, $180^{\circ}$.

blocks.prompt: One Lewis formula of the nitrite ion, $\ce{NO2^-}$, has one $\ce{N=O}$ bond, one $\ce{N-O}$ bond and a lone pair on nitrogen. What is the hybridization of nitrogen?
blocks.hint: The double bond is one domain. Don't forget the lone pair.
blocks.explain: Two bonds and a lone pair make three domains: sp², and a bent ion. sp forgets the lone pair; sp³ counts the double bond twice.

blocks.text: $\sigma$ bond: head-on overlap, electron density on the bond axis. $\pi$ bond: sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals, density above and below the axis.
Single bond = 1 $\sigma$. Double bond = 1 $\sigma$ + 1 $\pi$. Triple bond = 1 $\sigma$ + 2 $\pi$.
A $\pi$ bond is usually weaker than a $\sigma$ bond, because sideways overlap is less effective.
sp³: 4 domains, tetrahedral, $109.5^{\circ}$. sp²: 3 domains, trigonal planar, $120^{\circ}$, one spare p. sp: 2 domains, linear, $180^{\circ}$, two spare p.
For sp, sp² and sp³ atoms: hybrid orbitals = $\sigma$ bonds + lone pairs. Lone pairs count; $\pi$ bonds don't.

mistakes: Counting a double bond as two $\sigma$ bonds. Only the first bond between two atoms is $\sigma$; the others are $\pi$.
Ignoring lone pairs when deducing hybridization. Count every domain: water's oxygen is sp³, not sp.
Counting a $\pi$ bond as an extra domain. A double bond is one domain, so the carbon in $\ce{CO2}$ is sp.
Putting $\pi$ density between the nuclei. That is the $\sigma$ bond; $\pi$ density is above and below the axis.
examTips: "Deduce" the number of $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds: draw the full structure and count bond by bond. Paper 1A options often match a miscount.
"Explain" a hybridization on Paper 2: which orbitals mix, how many hybrids, their shape and the bonds they form, one point per sentence.
"Describe" a $\pi$ bond: sideways overlap of p orbitals, density above and below the axis.
